source.title: From Human Cognition to Neural Activations: Probing the Computational Primitives of Spatial Reasoning in LLMs
source.authors: Jiyuan An; Liner Yang; Mengyan Wang; Luming Lu; Weihua An; Erhong Yang

record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAE analysis in LLMs to identify sparse, task-relevant features and reports reconstruction and feature-overlap results. This is a different method from the original toy-network superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: The SAE feature, sparsity, reconstruction, overlap, and SAE-ablation results are included. Behavioral accuracy, linear-probe scores, and activation-patching results are not rows: they do not measure the claim versions' feature-overlap or recoverability assertions. The paper does not test superposition geometry, feature-capacity competition, polysemanticity, or feature dimensionality.
record.test_reason: The study is about spatial reasoning in LLMs and uses SAEs only as a tool to find spatial features. Table 4 reports its own SAEs' reconstruction and sparsity as a quality check, not as evidence about superposition. The overlap figures compare spatial feature sets across tasks and languages; they do not test whether SAE features are stable or canonical across SAE training runs. No result bears on toy-model geometry, capacity, polysemanticity or feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude spatial information is encoded in intermediate layers and can causally influence behaviour. They add that these representations are transient, fragmented across tasks and weakly integrated into final predictions. Cross-language results show mechanistic degeneracy: similar behaviour arises from distinct internal pathways. They place LLMs between shallow pattern matching and robust spatial cognition.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes spatial representations in LLMs using probes, SAEs, attribution, and interventions; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported feature overlap differs across task-family comparisons and between activation-frequency and causal-attribution rankings across languages.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE-identified spatial features overlap only 12–18% across task families. Causally ranked features overlap substantially less across languages than frequency-ranked ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features supporting a given capability in LLMs are task- and language-specific rather than shared, and the apparent sharing depends on the ranking criterion (frequency vs attribution).

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says code will be published after acceptance)
record.problems: Evidence for SAE reconstruction and sparsity is reported for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in Table 4, while the model is not specified in some aggregate feature and ablation statements. Feature overlap is not quantified for the cross-linguistic causal-attribution comparison. The paper itself notes that causal interventions provide only partial causal characterization and that analyses focus on linearly decodable information.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported SAE metric or overlap result omitted. Other behavioral, probing, and patching results were left out because they do not directly measure the feature-recovery or feature-canonicality assertions in the tested versions.

untested.parts: All; no capacity or importance analysis.
Whether features are spread across neurons, or whether SAE recovery is evidence of superposition. SAE metrics are reported only as tool quality checks.
Completeness, seed or run stability, and canonicality of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: The record over-claimed V4/V5 tests; SAEs here are an instrument. Table 4 internals look inconsistent: MSE 0.798 with R² 0.9965, and about 300k–420k training tokens versus 300–400 batches of 4,096 tokens. The model is unstated for the overlap and ablation results. Elhage et al. 2022 is cited only in related work.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether feature competition for limited capacity causes polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions by importance.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.
Whether features are spread across many neurons; SAE recoverability is tested only for spatial features in the reported analysis, not broadly across LLMs or architectures.
Completeness, stability across random seeds or checkpoints, and whether SAE features are canonical units beyond the reported task-family and language comparisons.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

relation.reason: The study applies SAE feature analysis and interventions to spatial reasoning without assessing superposition, capacity-driven polysemanticity, dictionary canonicality, or feature dimensionality.

tranche.reason: SAEs serve as tools for studying spatial computation. Table 4 reports tool quality; task and language overlaps characterize spatial pathways, without testing the catalog's superposition claims.

source_check.notes: All sampled values match the cited text or Table 4. The prose below Table 4 incorrectly gives maximum MSE as 0.798; the table includes 0.823 for Task 2 ZH.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The SAE results report sparse activations, strong reconstruction metrics, spatially selective features, and task-specific ablation effects (R1, R4–R41). The control ablation had negligible effect (R42).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Feature overlap across task families is limited, and overlap is lower when features are ranked by causal attribution across languages; the study does not establish SAE features as universally shared units (R2–R3).
